title: Planning licks across the choruses
summary: Ridgley says the whole sixteen bars were thought out ahead, with everyone playing something even during a solo.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: When you start out a melody line, while we're talking about Marilyn, my Marilyn, we just keep sticking with that so all my questions would be about that. Would you, when we're just starting out like bum bum bum bum, would you see in your mind ahead of time all of these licks that you plan to use all the way through the sixteen measures, or would you just see the one that you're going to use immediately?

You'd rather have that in mind. For the whole sixteen measures before you even get going? You know, you practice that and you've got it in mind, you know you're going to do it. I see. Well, when I was after you to do that, you see.

Right. You wouldn't, you wouldn't say one beat ahead of when it was time for your lick, you wouldn't, you wouldn't be up in the air as to which lick you were going to use. You would already have had it in your mind ahead of time what lick you were going to use.
Oh yes, for sure. I see. You'd get up, you'd get up, up, up and down, you know.
You had it all thought out before you got going.
You see, you've got that in mind when I told you I'd, you would practice it. Right. You'd know what you're going to do.
And the band for example would handle five or six, how many choruses would you have? Say you're going to play Maryland, would it be five or seven or something other times through?

Well, Maryland, now what you mean? Now we say that they did the trumpet, was playing the bugle part of it, I get to say. Well, suppose we would have to do eight bars, we'd repeat it. And sometimes we wouldn't repeat it because each fella had his part to play, you see. Then it wouldn't be as hard on the trumpet player. See, the clarinet would take each bar and the trombone, you see, would take their part and we had a good banjo, you see, or something like that. But we would all be doing something.
Even when the fellow had his solo?

Yeah, when he had his solo. See, we would all be doing something, but God keep it from being so empty. I see. I see. Now the player, the banjo player, he'd have his solo and I'd make the, you know, like that, and the clarinet, you know, gonna make it variations, what he's gonna do. But probably allowing the trumpet to catch a blow. And the piano would be carrying the melody, too. See.
And probably your first and your last time through the chorus, you'd all play louder?

All together, you see. Then we'd all, then the trombone would heavily lead to Maryland, you see, and the trumpet would be varied, you see, that's how I would stop. She'd be varied, I mean them bigger, go to the end, but the trombone would be buying down, you see.
Even the piano, she'd be buying down with the melody, too.
